title: Pongal / Onam (regional; harvest)
hook: a flower carpet that grows every morning for ten days, because a beloved king is coming home to check on his people

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first half of Pongal Onam: a new pot boiling over in the sun, and four days of thank-yous, cattle included. Who did you thank? Today, the other harvest, in Kerala. And a look back at the week. Day one hundred fifty-four.
screen: `PONGAL: MORE THAN THE POT CAN HOLD.`

segments.voice: In Kerala, in late summer, on the first morning of Onam, someone in the house gets up early and lays a small circle of flower petals on the ground at the front door. Yellow, orange, white. The next morning, the circle gets a ring bigger. And the next. For ten days it grows, a carpet of flowers called a pookalam, until by the last day it's a whole bright mandala of petals across the doorstep. Why all the trouble? Because a guest is coming. Not a god this time. A king. And he wants to see that his people are happy.
screen: `A CIRCLE OF PETALS AT THE DOOR.` → `BIGGER EVERY MORNING FOR TEN DAYS.` → `A KING IS COMING.`

segments.voice: The king is Mahabali, and he's an asura, from the side of the story usually cast as the gods' rivals. But in Kerala he's remembered as the best king there ever was. A Malayalam folk song still sung at Onam remembers his reign as a time when all people were equal: no lies, no cheating, no one poor. The gods grew worried about how powerful he'd become. So Vishnu came to him as Vamana, a small boy-priest, and asked for a gift: just as much land as he could cover in three steps. Bali, who never refused anyone, said yes. And the boy grew. One step covered the earth. The second covered the heavens. There was nowhere left for the third. So Bali bowed and offered his own head. Vamana's foot pressed him down into the world below. The Bhagavata Purana tells it as a story about Bali's devotion and generosity, and he's rewarded, not destroyed. In Kerala, the story adds something: Bali asked for one thing, to visit his people once a year. Onam is that visit. So everyone makes sure he'll find them well. The pookalam at the door. New clothes. And the Onam sadhya, a huge vegetarian feast served on a banana leaf, often more than twenty dishes, eaten together. Boat races on the backwaters. It's Kerala's harvest festival too, in the month of Chingam. And that's the week: Shivaratri's four watches and its pillar of light, Raksha Bandhan's thread, the sun turning at Sankranti, Pongal's pot, and now a king coming home. Different stories. Same instinct: make the day worth arriving for.
screen: `AN ASURA, THE BEST OF KINGS.` · `THREE STEPS: EARTH, HEAVEN, HIS HEAD.` · `ONE VISIT A YEAR: ONAM.` · `THE WEEK: VIGIL, THREAD, SUN, POT.` · then, large: `MAKE THE DAY WORTH ARRIVING FOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: get the house ready for Mahabali. Settle, and breathe. Imagine the king is visiting you this year, to see how you are. Not to judge. Just to see. What would you want him to find? Picture laying one ring of flower petals at your door for each thing that's good in your life right now. One ring. Then another. Then another. Let the circle grow, and don't rush it. When it's as big as it's going to get, just sit beside it, and breathe, like someone waiting for a guest they love. The bell holds the time.
Pongal and Onam. Two harvests: Tamil Nadu's pot boiling over for the sun, and Kerala's flower carpet for a king who comes home once a year.
Your line: Pongal and Onam, regional, harvest. Today, get one small thing ready for someone who's coming, as if they mattered most. Day one hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: During the ten days of Onam in the Malayalam month of Chingam, many Hindus in Kerala lay a pookalam of flowers at the door that grows each day, wear new clothes, and share the Onam sadhya on banana leaves to welcome King Mahabali on his yearly visit.

original.note: Malayalam: the name of Kerala's harvest festival, in the month of Chingam.

trapdoor: what you thought: a flower festival.
what it means: a harvest, and a homecoming: Kerala makes the house ready for the good king Mahabali's yearly visit.
what a scholar hears: the Vamana story is in the Bhagavata Purana; the yearly visit and the equal-kingdom song are Kerala's own.

notes: The folk song 'Maveli nadu vanidum kalam' is paraphrased, not quoted. Confirm the gloss (all equal, no lies, no cheating, no poverty).

Onam: ten days from Atham to Thiruvonam in Chingam (August–September); the pookalam grows daily. Confirm.
